Apparently, some idiots have suddenly started dumping memory stocks because of this post I made…

Yes, I posted it to warn people not to underestimate YMTC. But that doesn’t mean I was telling anyone to panic-sell.

NAND is still in short supply, and that shortage will persist.

NVIDIA’s CMX racks are currently so constrained by NAND shortages that they cannot even be shipped fully populated. Customers looking to purchase CMX racks are reportedly being asked to source some of the NAND themselves to fill the racks.

I’m not a NAND bear—let me be absolutely clear about that. YMTC is still heavily exposed to the consumer market, and it should not be underestimated. But that does not mean YMTC is going to push the NAND market into oversupply.

Recently, bearish notes and rumors on NAND appear to be circulating, particularly out of China, along with negative news related to QLC price negotiations.

A few points are worth clarifying.

It should come as no surprise that SanDisk would sign an LTA with Meta at a price below its initial quote. Among NAND manufacturers, SanDisk is the most proactive in securing LTAs and plans to allocate more than 50% of its total volume to such agreements. Given this strategy, SanDisk is clearly willing to accept LTA pricing below the prevailing quarterly contract price.

Accordingly, I believe it is unreasonable to extrapolate from this that SanDisk cannot seamlessly redirect the entire volume to higher-paying North American customers.

Chinese module makers were reportedly turned down when they attempted to sell more eSSDs to Chinese CSPs. My understanding is that this is because Chinese CSPs have direct procurement channels with YMTC.

There have also been recent reports that hyperscalers are pushing back against QLC eSSD prices, leaving some volume unabsorbed. However, my understanding is that neocloud providers have sufficient demand to absorb this volume.

With memory stocks performing poorly, negative headlines seem to be gaining even more traction. I remain bullish on memory.

REUTERS: SAMSUNG AND SK HYNIX ARE EXPLORING THE ADOPTION OF CHINESE-MADE EQUIPMENT AS U.S. SANCTIONS COULD MAKE IT MORE DIFFICULT TO BRING EQUIPMENT INTO THEIR CHINA FABS

According to Reuters sources, the two companies began testing AMEC’s etching equipment about two years ago, although no decision has yet been made on broader deployment.

The aim is not to expand production capacity in China, but to keep Chinese suppliers in reserve in case U.S. restrictions are extended to the servicing, repair, or replacement of existing Western equipment.

Samsung operates a NAND plant in Xi’an, while SK Hynix operates a DRAM plant in Wuxi and NAND facilities in Dalian. These plants currently rely heavily on etching equipment from U.S. suppliers such as Applied Materials and Lam Research.

AMEC’s equipment is already used by Chinese chipmakers including YMTC. Chinese tools are about 20% to 30% cheaper than comparable foreign equipment, while the technology gap has also narrowed in areas such as etching, deposition, cleaning, and planarization.

Approval from Samsung or SK Hynix would provide AMEC with significant technical and commercial validation and could, over the longer term, pose a threat to established global equipment suppliers such as Applied Materials, Lam Research, and KLA.

According to DigiTimes, YMTC and CXMT are seeking to increase the share of their memory supply shipped outside China.

As part of this strategy, YMTC is reportedly selling NAND chips to independent third-party module makers, which then assemble them into finished enterprise solid-state drives (SSDs) for customers such as U.S. neocloud providers. This indirect route is intended to avoid sensitivities surrounding the products’ country of origin.

YMTC’s new Phase 3 fab was originally scheduled to begin mass production in the second quarter of 2027, but the start of operations is now expected to be brought forward to the fourth quarter of 2026. The fab will have a total production capacity of 100,000 wafers per month and is expected to initially operate at around 50,000 wafers per month. Notably, YMTC plans to allocate 20% of the fab’s capacity to LPDDR trial production, making it the company’s first DRAM manufacturing base.

Supply-chain sources said that amid the continued global memory shortage, China’s two major memory manufacturers have been tasked with raising the domestic market’s self-sufficiency rate. China’s memory self-sufficiency rate could exceed 50% as early as late 2027 or sometime in 2028.

As production capacity at YMTC’s Wuhan Phase 3 fab begins to ramp up meaningfully from 2027, the company is expected to continue pursuing a strategy of increasing the share of its supply shipped to overseas markets.

YMTC is not alone in making this move. With DDR5 and LPDDR5 supplies becoming increasingly tight, CXMT has reportedly begun product qualification with small and midsized cloud service providers in markets including the U.S. and Canada. The company appears to be seeking to secure customers early by locking in capacity commitments ahead of time.

Industry sources said that it is currently “possible in principle” for private-sector U.S. companies to purchase products from YMTC or CXMT.

Recent reports that Apple is seeking to incorporate more production capacity from Chinese memory suppliers into its supply chain have drawn market attention. However, supply-chain industry sources believe that Apple’s influence is no longer what it once was in the AI era and that its impact on industry-wide supply and demand has declined substantially.

From the perspective of Chinese suppliers, entering Apple’s supply chain would primarily serve as proof that the quality of their products has reached the level of major global vendors. They reportedly have no intention of supplying Apple in large volumes or competing by cutting prices.

According to industry sources, some of Apple’s procurement personnel have also recently moved to NVIDIA.

Even if Apple attempts to use CXMT’s or YMTC’s capacity to lower its procurement prices, it is unlikely to succeed in 2026. Moreover, only limited capacity reportedly remains available for allocation in 2027.

Korean media reported that SK hynix’s NAND flash business continues to struggle to narrow the productivity gap with Samsung Electronics and other competitors, as it lags in transitioning older production lines to newer process generations.

As of the second quarter of this year, older-generation processes such as 176-layer NAND still accounted for more than half of SK hynix’s production, while Samsung Electronics had already completed the transition of its main production generation to 236-layer NAND.

The 176-layer generation currently accounts for around 50% of SK hynix’s NAND production in the second quarter. This high dependence on 176-layer NAND puts the company at a cost disadvantage because it produces relatively fewer bits per wafer.

Some analysts also say that although SK hynix has emphasized progress on its technology roadmap, including expanding the share of 300-layer-class NAND, this has yet to translate clearly into revenue performance.

NAND flash improves both capacity and cost efficiency by vertically stacking memory cells that store data. The greater the number of layers, the more data can be stored on a wafer of the same area, improving both output per wafer and cost competitiveness. Companies that fail to migrate to next-generation processes must therefore use more wafers and devote more production-line operating time to produce the same volume, inevitably placing them at a disadvantage in terms of profitability.

As of the end of the second quarter, 236-layer NAND accounted for more than 60% of Samsung Electronics’ production, establishing it as the company’s main production generation. Although both SK hynix and Samsung Electronics have NAND generations in the low-to-mid-200-layer range, there is a clear gap in the speed at which they have transitioned to mass production.

“Samsung Electronics is pursuing a strategy of concentrating production volumes in a specific generation to improve both yields and costs, whereas SK hynix operates multiple generations simultaneously, which inevitably reduces the relative efficiency of its production-line operations,” an industry official said.

SK hynix’s current NAND production structure also trails those of Micron and China’s YMTC, in addition to Samsung Electronics. According to market research firm Omdia, as of the end of the second quarter, 232-layer NAND accounted for 53% of Micron’s production, while the next-generation 276-layer product had expanded to 33%. At YMTC, 232-layer NAND represented 68% of production, indicating that the company had already established a production system centered on advanced processes.

At Kioxia and Sandisk, 162-layer BiCS6 accounted for 37% of production and 112-layer BiCS5 for 34% as of the second quarter, meaning older-generation processes still made up roughly 70% of total production. While their generation mix may appear similar to that of SK hynix, the share of their latest-generation BiCS8, a 218-layer product, nearly tripled in just two quarters, rising from 9% in the fourth quarter of last year to 24% in the second quarter of this year. Their transition pace is therefore considered relatively fast.

This trend is also evident in revenue market share.

According to industry sources, SK hynix’s NAND revenue share, including Solidigm, rose to 21.4% in the fourth quarter of last year before plunging by nearly 5 percentage points to 16.4% in the first quarter of this year. Over the same period, China’s YMTC increased its share from 11.5% to 16.2%, nearly catching up with SK hynix. Some interpret this as evidence that SK hynix may have had relatively limited capacity to respond with additional volumes during a period of rising NAND prices.

“When prices are rising, a higher share of newer-generation products allows increases in selling prices to combine with cost improvements, producing a greater uplift in profit margins,” an industry official said. “SK hynix’s market-share decline should be viewed not simply as a volume issue, but as the result of delays in its process-generation transition.”

The official added, however, that “given the recent continued rise in NAND prices, the impact on the company’s overall earnings is limited.”
